neighbours.label: Words for places where land is dug, mined or worked over (pits, quarries, slag heaps, reclamation, shoveling); best guess from a weak, mixed card
fire: Along the ridge the miners left a row of abandoned clay pits and quarries.
The children played near the old sand pits and stone quarries above the river.
Much of the airport stands on ground won by land reclamation from the bay.
The hills behind the smelter are covered with tailings and slag heaps.
My uncle hurt his back shoveling gravel onto the track last spring.
The moor is pocked with peat pits and old lime quarries.
Decades of coastal reclamation pushed the shoreline a mile out to sea.
The road passes worked-out chalk pits and marble quarries on both sides.
quiet: Along the ridge the hikers left a row of painted signs and markers.
The children played near the old stone bridge and the mill above the river.
Much of the airport stands on ground bought by the city from the railway.
The hills behind the school are covered with heather and tall pines.
My uncle hurt his back carrying boxes up the stairs last spring.
The moor is crossed by footpaths and old stone walls.
Decades of careful planning kept the shoreline open to walkers.
The road passes white cottages and small chapels on both sides.

notes: Card top examples mix English land-working words (charcoal pits, flower farms, land reclamation, shoveling) with French past participles (évacué, mangé). Probes: quarries 0.40, reclamation 0.22, shoveling 0.21, slag heaps 0.20, a French participle 0.06. The label covers only the English part and fires weakly; expect a marginal result.
